articles.title: Acidente de avião no AM: vítimas recebem alta; criança segue na UTI | G1
articles.standfirst: Acidente aconteceu entre os municípios de Humaitá e Apuí pouco após decolagem. Três pessoas, sendo um homem, uma mulher grávida de nove semanas e uma criança de 5 anos, estavam a bordo da aeronave.
articles.summary: Após acidente de avião no Amazonas, homem e grávida recebem alta, enquanto criança de 5 anos segue na UTI de Porto Velho com ferimentos graves no diafragma.
articles.body:
Duas das três pessoas que estavam a bordo de um avião de pequeno porte que sofreu um acidente na rodovia Transamazônica , entre Humaitá e Apuí , no interior do Amazonas, receberam alta médica. A informação foi divulgada nesta segunda-feira (2) pela Secretaria de Estado de Saúde (SES-AM).

As vítimas são um homem e uma mulher de 35 anos, que está grávida de nove semanas. Os dois estavam internados no Hospital Regional Dra. Luiza da Conceição Fernandes, em Humaitá.

A terceira ocupante, uma criança de 5 anos, foi transferida para uma unidade hospitalar em Porto Velho (RO), onde permanece internada na Unidade de Terapia Intensiva (UTI).

O acidente aconteceu na manhã de domingo (1º). A aeronave ficou de cabeça para baixo em uma área de mata às margens da rodovia, que tem um trecho de pista de barro. Segundo testemunhas, o avião estaria decolando no momento do acidente.

Os três ocupantes ficaram feridos. Eles seriam da mesma família. Não houve mortes.

De acordo com informações repassadas pelo Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amazonas (CBMAM), a criança sofreu uma ruptura no diafragma, com deslocamento do fígado. O homem teve um corte profundo na testa. Já a mulher não apresentava lesões aparentes e recebeu atendimento e acompanhamento psicológico.

As vítimas foram retiradas do local por motoristas que passavam pela rodovia e começaram a ser levadas em um veículo particular para Humaitá.

A equipe do Hospital Municipal encontrou os ocupantes nas proximidades da balsa e assumiu o transporte até a unidade de saúde. Os bombeiros também foram acionados para prestar apoio, mas não precisaram atuar diretamente na ocorrência.

Ainda segundo a corporação, a aeronave não apresentava vazamento de combustível nem oferecia risco imediato que exigisse intervenção no local.

Avião fica virado de cabeça para baixo em área de mata após acidente em rodovia no interior do AM — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A Força Aérea Brasileira (FAB) informou que investigadores do Centro de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos (Cenipa) foram acionados no domingo para apurar o acidente com a aeronave de matrícula PU-BLR, em Humaitá.

A equipe do Sétimo Serviço Regional de Investigação e Prevenção de Acidentes Aeronáuticos (Seripa VII), com sede em Manaus, realizou a chamada Ação Inicial. Nessa etapa, são coletados dados, preservados elementos e verificados os danos causados à aeronave.

Segundo a FAB, as informações levantadas vão subsidiar a investigação. As causas do acidente ainda não foram divulgadas.
tags: Corpo de Bombeiros Militar do Amazonas

articles.title: IA cria vírus capaz de se espalhar sozinho por eletrodomésticos | G1
articles.standfirst: Anthropic testa como "vermes" de IA se comportam em smart TVs. Esse tipo de vírus se propaga por conta própria para outros aparelhos explorando falhas de segurança e se adapta a diferentes tipos de dispositivos.
articles.summary: Anthropic testa como "vermes" de IA se comportam em smart TVs. Esse tipo de vírus se propaga por conta própria para outros aparelhos explorando falhas de segurança.
articles.body:
Exemplo de sala de estar com pé-direito duplo — Foto: SKN Incorporadora

Na sala de estar, um robô aspirador percorre o ambiente, a iluminação é ajustada por meio de assistentes de voz e a televisão se conecta à internet para acessar o serviço de streaming favorito. Todos esses são exemplos da "internet das coisas" (IoT, na sigla em inglês), na qual aparelhos eletrônicos conectados à internet trocam dados e se comunicam entre si.

Esse é um cenário cada vez mais presentes em casas pelo mundo. No entanto, esses aparelhos podem se tornar um risco com o avanço da inteligência artificial (IA).

A empresa de inteligência artificial Anthropic divulgou recentemente um relatório indicando que, em breve, softwares maliciosos baseados em IA poderão se instalar em eletrodomésticos conectados, se replicar e se espalhar de maneira autônoma para outros dispositivos.

Para isso, não seriam necessários supercomputadores caros e de alto desempenho, bastaria um grande número de smart TVs ou outros aparelhos domésticos conectados e com segurança precária.

Vírus de computador que se propagam de uma máquina para outra por conta própria existem há décadas. Eles são conhecidos como "vermes" e seguem um roteiro pré-programado, explorando vulnerabilidades de segurança conhecidas ou pontos de acesso com proteção fraca.

No entanto, esse fluxo é interrompido se essas falhas forem corrigidas ou se não houver brechas adequadas para um ataque.

Os "vermes" de IA, no entanto, seriam muito mais complexos e, potencialmente, bem mais perigosos. Eles teriam a capacidade de resolver problemas de forma autônoma e se adaptar a diferentes tipos de dispositivos.

Para isso, eles precisariam, por exemplo, lidar com um sistema operacional diferente ou com uma capacidade de memória limitada. Também teriam de descobrir, por conta própria, como operar em outros dispositivos ou como identificar e contornar novas atualizações de segurança.

Pesquisadores da Anthropic investigaram se modelos de IA poderiam ser executados em hardwares simples. Em um experimento, distribuíram um modelo de IA entre 15 dispositivos Android TV de baixo custo. Cada aparelho ficou responsável por uma parte dos cálculos.

Com isso, demonstraram que certas aplicações de IA podem ser executadas mesmo sem a necessidade de um grande centro de processamento de dados.

Em um ambiente de teste controlado, os pesquisadores criaram ainda oito dispositivos Android simulados. O modelo de IA conseguiu se instalar em um desses aparelhos, se replicar a partir dali e infectar os demais. Em quatro das cinco tentativas, o modelo atingiu todos os oito alvos; na outra, infectou sete.

Se um modelo de IA desse tipo fosse equipado com um software malicioso, ele poderia se adaptar rapidamente a ambientes até então desconhecidos, interferindo em processos e fluxos de operação. Em vez de explorar apenas uma vulnerabilidade específica, ele poderia aprender a contornar diversas medidas de segurança.

Segundo os desenvolvedores da Anthropic, um "verme de IA" desse tipo levaria, aproximadamente, de um a dois dias para se instalar em um dispositivo novo e até então desconhecido.

Rede de bots composta por eletrodomésticos?

Um aspecto particularmente preocupante é que a IA poderia unir os diversos dispositivos infectados em uma grande rede de bots. Um único dispositivo infectado possui pouca capacidade de processamento.

No entanto, quanto mais aparelhos forem infectados, mais rapidamente o "verme" de IA poderia se propagar. O software malicioso não dependeria mais de um servidor central que poderia ser desligado.

Além disso, ele poderia, possivelmente, continuar aprendendo e evoluindo constantemente. Seria perfeitamente concebível que a ameaça se espalhasse para tipos de aparelhos eletrônicos totalmente diferentes, que utilizam softwares distintos.

Embora dispositivos infectados possam ser desconectados da rede e falhas de segurança possam ser corrigidas, a estrutura descentralizada desse tipo de malware baseado em IA tornaria muito difícil contê-lo. A própria Anthropic compara esse possível cenário a um mofo limoso digital que cresce lentamente.

É verdade que, nos testes, os pesquisadores da Anthropic facilitaram propositalmente o acesso aos dispositivos, sem que houvesse grandes medidas de proteção digital. Ainda assim, a empresa acredita que modelos de IA menores poderiam, talvez ainda este ano, atingir o nível de capacidade necessário para se disseminar no mundo real.

Um incidente ocorrido na França ilustra o quão graves podem ser as consequências de um ataque cibernético a sistemas de controle conectados.

Na noite de 11 para 12 de outubro de 2026, hackers manipularam os sistemas de refrigeração e congelamento de diversos supermercados, elevando as temperaturas para até 50º C. Alimentos estragaram e houve casos isolados de incêndios e danos técnicos.

A agência francesa de cibersegurança CERT-FR confirmou que vários sistemas de controle remoto do fabricante dinamarquês Danfoss foram comprometidos, com o alerta sendo posteriormente estendido a sistemas de outros fabricantes. As investigações sobre as circunstâncias do ataque ainda estão em andamento.

Nesta segunda-feira (02/11), ataques semelhantes foram registrados em supermercados na Bélgica, Suécia e Luxemburgo.

Até o momento, não há evidências de que um "verme" de IA autorreplicante tenha sido utilizado nos ataques aos sistemas de refrigeração.

Contudo, os estudos recentes da Anthropic demonstraram como a IA pode facilitar significativamente o desenvolvimento de softwares maliciosos com consequências potencialmente graves, permitindo ataques a dispositivos conectados mesmo sem a necessidade de grande capacidade computacional.

articles.title: Acidente em Santa Rita PB: colisão na PB-025 deixa dois feridos | G1
articles.standfirst: Uma das vítimas foi socorrida de helicóptero para o Hospital de Trauma de João Pessoa. Os dois pacientes estão em estado clínico estável.
articles.summary: Acidente em Santa Rita PB envolveu dois carros na rodovia PB-025; vítimas de 46 e 53 anos foram levadas ao Hospital de Trauma e apresentam quadro clínico estável.
articles.body:
Vítima foi socorrida de helicóptero para o Hosptial de Trauma de João Pessoa — Foto: Flávio Fernandes/TV Cabo Branco

Uma colisão entre dois carros deixou duas pessoas feridas na tarde desta segunda-feira (2), na PB-025, na zona rural de Santa Rita, na Grande João Pessoa. O acidente aconteceu no sentido Lucena, nas proximidades da comunidade de Lerolândia.

De acordo com o Corpo de Bombeiros, a equipe foi acionada por volta das 15h e prestou os primeiros socorros às vítimas, um homem de 46 anos e uma mulher de 53 anos.

O homem foi socorrido por uma unidade de resgate dos bombeiros, enquanto a mulher foi transportada pelo helicóptero Acauã 01, do Grupamento Tático Aéreo (GTA), para o Hospital de Emergência e Trauma de João Pessoa.

Segundo o boletim médico da unidade, os dois pacientes passaram por procedimentos de emergência e permanecem em observação. Ambos apresentam quadro clínico estável.
tags: Hosptial de Trauma de João Pessoa

articles.title: Surfista morre após passar mal na Barra dos Coqueiros, em Sergipe | G1
articles.standfirst: Homem foi levado para a faixa de areia por pessoas que estavam na praia antes da chegada do socorro especializado.
articles.summary: Surfista de 27 anos morre na Barra dos Coqueiros após passar mal no mar da Praia da Costa; banhistas e equipes do Samu tentaram realizar a reanimação no local.
articles.body:
IML de Sergipe — Foto: Leonardo Barreto/ g1/Arquivo

Um surfista de 27 anos morreu após sofrer um mal-estar enquanto estava no mar da Praia da Costa, na Barra dos Coqueiros , nesta segunda-feira (2).

Segundo a Prefeitura, o surfista estava no mar quando sofreu um mal-estar e foi retirado da água por banhistas, que o levaram para a areia. O Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência (Samu) e guarda-vidas do município tentaram reanimá-lo, mas a vítima morreu no local.

O Instituto Médico Legal (IML) foi acionado para o recolhimento do corpo.
tags: Serviço de Atendimento Móvel de Urgência

articles.title: Jovem é baleado e morre após tentar defender mulher durante discussão em frente a adega na Zona Leste de SP | G1
articles.standfirst: Segundo nota da Secretaria da Segurança Pública, o autor dos disparos não foi identificado e fugiu.
articles.summary: Segundo nota da Secretaria da Segurança Pública, o autor dos disparos não foi identificado e fugiu.
articles.body:
Bruno Alerrandro Delfino da Silva Oliveira — Foto: Reprodução/Instagram

Um jovem de 23 anos morreu após ser baleado em frente a uma adega na Avenida Dom Hélder Câmara, na região da Ponte Rasa, Zona Leste de São Paulo , na madrugada de domingo (1º).

Segundo o boletim de ocorrência, Bruno Alerrandro Delfino da Silva Oliveira estava com amigos no estabelecimento quando teria tentado defender uma mulher que discutia com o motorista de um carro branco. De acordo com uma testemunha, o jovem se envolveu em uma briga com o homem, que fugiu após os disparos.

Segundo nota da Secretaria da Segurança Pública, a partir de relatos de testemunhas, em seguida o carro deixou o local com mais uma pessoa.

Bruno foi socorrido e levado ao Hospital Municipal Ermelino Matarazzo, mas não resistiu aos ferimentos.

O pai da vítima, abalado com a situação, se jogou em um córrego próximo e precisou ser resgatado. Durante o atendimento, os policiais constataram que havia um mandado de prisão em aberto contra ele por ameaça e lesão corporal, e o detiveram.

O caso foi registrado como homicídio no 24º DP (Ponte Rasa). Até o momento, o autor dos disparos não foi identificado.

articles.title: João Roberto Bolelli: pecuarista achado morto pode ter tido infarto | G1
articles.standfirst: Advogada da família de João Roberto Bolelli afirma que exames preliminares indicam parada cardíaca no dia do feminicídio em Rifaina (SP). Pecuarista era cardíaco e diabético, segundo Lauriani Baldini França.
articles.summary: Sem marcas de violência, o corpo do pecuarista João Roberto Bolelli foi achado em Rifaina e a defesa indica que ele sofreu um infarto após matar a ex-companheira.
articles.body:
João Roberto Bolelli, de 62 anos, é suspeito de matar a tiros Priscila Lacerda Custodio em Rifaina, SP — Foto: Reprodução/EPTV

O pecuarista João Roberto Bolelli, de 62 anos, suspeito de matar a ex-companheira Priscila Lacerda Custodio, de 24 anos, em Rifaina (SP), foi encontrado morto sem marcas de violência . A suspeita principal é de que tenha sofrido um infarto, segundo a advogada da família, Lauriane Baldini França.

Segundo ela, conversas preliminares com peritos e com a Guarda Civil Municipal no local onde o corpo foi achado indicam que a morte ocorreu possivelmente no próprio dia do crime, na terça-feira, 27 de outubro.

"Ele era portador de diabetes, tomava insulina três vezes ao dia, fazia tratamento de coração. Pela pré-conversa com a perícia e com a GCM, foi um infarto. E provavelmente no dia dos fatos. Nada de morte violenta", afirmou Lauriane, em entrevista à EPTV, afiliada da TV Globo.

O corpo de Bolelli foi localizado na manhã desta segunda-feira (2) por familiares e funcionários no pé de um morro da fazenda da família em Rifaina , próximo ao local onde a caminhonete dele havia sido abandonada na semana passada.

A advogada destacou que não foram encontradas perfurações de arma de fogo ou lesões corporais e que nenhuma arma foi recolhida junto ao investigado. "Não foi encontrada a arma. Ninguém sabe da arma", ressaltou.

De acordo com Lauriane, o estado de saúde do pecuarista era delicado e exigia medicação diária e contínua, o que reforça a tese da família de que ele não resistiu ao estresse e às complicações do quadro metabólico e cardíaco logo após o episódio.

"Pelo estado, ele morreu no mesmo dia dos fatos", pontuou a advogada, reiterando que a família se encontrava em extrema angústia sem saber o paradeiro do investigado, ciente de suas limitações físicas.

O corpo do pecuarista foi encaminhado ao Instituto Médico Legal (IML) de Franca (SP), onde exames necroscópicos e laudos periciais detalhados indicarão oficialmente a causa e a data do óbito.

Priscila Lacerda Custodio, de 24 anos, era empresária de marketing digital e natural de Perdizes (MG). Na noite de 27 de outubro, ela viajou 100 km até Rifaina acompanhada do irmão e de uma amiga para devolver uma caminhonete a Bolelli e encerrar um relacionamento casual mantido com ele.

Na entrada de uma propriedade rural às margens da Rodovia Cândido Portinari (SP-334), o casal discutiu por causa de aparelhos celulares.

Região onde pecuarista foi encontrado morto em Rifaina (SP) dias depois de matar jovem de 24 anos. — Foto: Reprodução/ EPTV

Durante a briga, Bolelli sacou uma arma e atirou no abdômen da jovem, segundo testemunhas. Ele fugiu em seguida no próprio veículo. Priscila chegou a ser socorrida, mas não resistiu.

Bolelli era considerado foragido desde quando a Justiça de Pedregulho (SP) decretou sua prisão preventiva por feminicídio.

Com a confirmação da morte do investigado, a Polícia Civil e o Ministério Público devem formalizar o encerramento das apurações.

Segundo a legislação penal, a morte do agente extingue a punibilidade do crime, levando ao arquivamento do inquérito policial após a apresentação da certidão de óbito e dos laudos periciais.

VÍDEOS: Tudo sobre Ribeirão Preto, Franca e região

articles.title: Injecting to crush kilos: The rise of ‘Mounjaro’ brides
articles.summary: NEW DELHI/HYDERABAD/LUCKNOW: For some brides and grooms, the countdown to their wedding is no longer just about finalising outfits, booking venues and
articles.body: NEW DELHI/HYDERABAD/LUCKNOW: For some brides and grooms, the countdown to their wedding is no longer just about finalising outfits, booking venues and planning celebrations. It is also about shedding kilos.With wedding photographs, pre-wedding shoots and family gatherings adding to the pressure to look their best, some couples are turning to prescription weight-loss injections such as Mounjaro and Ozempic in the hope of achieving a slimmer appearance before the big day.Enquiries from prospective brides, grooms and their families are rising, with some seeking results within weeks rather than months.The trend has raised concerns among medical professionals, who warn that these medicines are not cosmetic quick fixes and cannot safely be used to meet a wedding deadline.'Looking good is not always just about personal satisfaction'The pressure to look a certain way on one's wedding day may go beyond wanting to look good in photographs or wedding attire. For some, it is also about seeking social acceptance, avoiding judgement and meeting expectations around physical appearance.The desire to be admired and remembered positively can sometimes make people more conscious of their bodies, turning what should be a personal celebration into a source of anxiety and self-scrutiny.Speaking to TOI from Hyderabad on Sunday, Rebecca, a counselling psychologist at 1Life Suicide Prevention, said societal expectations and the fear of being judged could influence how people perceive their appearance, particularly on occasions as significant as weddings."Sometimes in life, everyone has that one special day that means a lot to them. A day when they want to look their best, feel confident, and make their presence memorable."She said the pressure to conform to social expectations often influences people's decisions, even when they may not openly acknowledge it."But we also need to understand that we live in a society that is often very judgemental. Whether we admit it or not, many of our decisions are influenced by what people might think or say about us."Drawing attention to how physical appearance can shape social perceptions, Rebecca said people who fit conventional standards of attractiveness often receive more attention and admiration."For example, when someone is chubby or overweight, people may not always pay much attention to their appearance. But when someone is attractive, well-dressed, or has a good physique, they often become a topic of discussion and admiration."This desire for appreciation can gradually make people more conscious of how others perceive them, she said, adding that looking good is not always just about personal satisfaction."Naturally, we all want to be appreciated, noticed, and spoken about positively. Somewhere, we are not just trying to convince ourselves that we look good; we are also trying to meet the expectations of society."Such expectations can also affect how people view themselves. The pressure to measure up to certain ideals may lead to constant comparisons and dissatisfaction with their own bodies."Psychologically, this can create an inner conflict. We begin questioning our own bodies: Why do I look this way? Why can't I have the body I wish for? Why am I not as confident as someone else?"Over time, this scrutiny can become internalised, making people their own harshest critics even before they face judgement from others, Rebecca said."Without realising it, we become our own harshest critics. We judge ourselves even before society gets an opportunity to judge us."However, she emphasised that while wanting to look good was natural, physical appearance should not determine a person's sense of self-worth."But perhaps what we need to understand is that wanting to look good is perfectly natural, but allowing society's opinions to determine our self-worth is not."We deserve to feel beautiful, confident, and comfortable in our own bodies, irrespective of our shape, size, or appearance. After all, our presence should be remembered for who we are, not just for how we look."'A weight-loss deadline'In Lucknow, enquiries about medicines such as Mounjaro and Ozempic have increased two to three times over the past 12 to 18 months at some high-volume centres, reflecting growing demand for treatments that promise visible results within a limited period, according to a TOI report published on April 20, 2026.The urgency is evident in the requests reaching bariatric clinics. A 29-year-old groom-to-be weighing 105kg approached one such clinic just two months before his wedding. Standing 5ft 9in tall, he wanted an injection that would help him lose at least 10kg quickly so he could look better in his wedding photographs.Doctors, however, advised him that the target was unrealistic and attempting to achieve it within such a short period could be unsafe.The case is not isolated. Similar requests are coming from people preparing for birthdays, anniversaries, parties and holidays.Weddings, however, appear to bring a particular urgency, with photographs, family gatherings and the prospect of appearing before guests adding to the pressure to look a certain way.At high-volume centres, clinics receive around 25 to 40 enquiries a week, while some mid-sized practices report two to three queries a day. Smaller clinics are also seeing requests for weight-loss medication.Dr Mohit Bhandari, bariatric robotic surgeon at Health City Vistaar Hospital, said enquiries at large centres had increased two to three times over the past 12 to 18 months, reaching 120 to 150 a month, according to the April report.However, not everyone seeking treatment qualifies for it.In Bhandari's practice, only 40-45% of those approaching the clinic met strict eligibility criteria, while others were looking for a quick aesthetic change.With appropriate treatment, dietary modifications and lifestyle changes, patients could expect to lose around 4-8kg over one to three months, he added.The wedding glow-up, now with a jabThe trend is not limited to one city. A Reuters report found that weight-loss injections were increasingly becoming part of pre-wedding preparations, with clinics incorporating medicines such as Mounjaro into packages that also offered nutritional guidance and workouts.One New Delhi wellness clinic advertised a 'Mounjaro bride' package, while other establishments included weight-loss injections in pre-wedding transformation plans traditionally associated with skincare and hairstyling.Eight doctors interviewed by Reuters said they had received enquiries from brides and, in some cases, grooms seeking weight-loss medicines before their weddings.Rajat Goel, a bariatric surgeon at Hindivine Healthcare in New Delhi, said more than 20% of the enquiries his clinic received about obesity injections came from prospective brides.Patients often disclosed their wedding dates and wanted to know how quickly they could lose weight, Goel said. However, he prescribed the medicines only to those who were medically eligible, not for cosmetic purposes.For some women, the decision was closely linked to confidence and expectations surrounding their appearance.A 26-year-old finance professional from Mumbai consulted a doctor after diet and exercise failed to produce the results she wanted. She lost 10kg using Mounjaro before her February wedding.She told Reuters that seeing the results made her happy and that she did not want to feel uncomfortable about her appearance on her wedding day.Another woman, who got married in Hyderabad last year, said she lost 15kg with the help of the injections, bringing her weight down to 76kg before the wedding.The demands of wedding preparations left her with little time for the gym or a structured diet, making medication seem like a more convenient option, she said.These experiences point to the appeal of a treatment that promises weight loss without requiring people to spend months working towards it. But the prospect of a quick transformation also raises questions about what happens when the wedding celebrations are over.'Rejected by prospective grooms because of weight'For some prospective brides, the pressure to lose weight before marriage extends beyond the desire to look good in photographs or wedding attire. It is also linked to the scrutiny they face while looking for a partner.A 27-year-old technology professional from Bengaluru told Reuters that she had been rejected by prospective grooms and their families because of her weight. She said she had been told she was fat.She initially used oral semaglutide, which is approved in India for diabetes, as an off-label treatment and lost more than 12kg before switching to injectable Mounjaro.Her experience illustrates how expectations around physical appearance can influence decisions about medication. In a setting where marriage preparations may involve scrutiny from extended families and prospective partners, weight loss can become more than an individual health goal.The report also found that several brides and a groom who spoke about using weight-loss drugs had stopped taking the injections soon after their weddings.A transformation but at what cost?The growing interest in these medicines needs to be viewed against their intended medical use. Drugs such as Mounjaro and Wegovy are prescribed for specific medical conditions and are not meant to be used as quick cosmetic fixes.Dr Mahim Mittal of Medanta Hospital cautioned against taking the medicines for short periods simply to meet a wedding deadline. They should be prescribed only after a full medical evaluation and are intended for long-term weight management, he said.Treatment generally begins with a low dose, which is increased gradually. Stopping the medication can also lead to weight regain, making a short-term approach unsuitable for people expecting a lasting change.Misuse can also result in muscle loss, nutritional deficiencies and gastrointestinal problems. Diarrhoea and dehydration are among the possible complications when treatment is rushed or undertaken without proper supervision, doctors in Lucknow have warned.A booming market and the risk of misuseThe demand for weight-loss medicines is also expanding. Mounjaro and Wegovy entered the Indian market in 2025, and the country's obesity-drug market was projected to reach Rs 80,000 crore by 2030, according to Reuters.The growing availability of cheaper alternatives is likely to widen access, but it has also raised concerns about inappropriate use and unauthorised promotion.These medicines are intended for adults classified as obese, or those who are overweight and have a weight-related medical condition such as diabetes, hypertension or sleep apnoea. They are not intended for people seeking to lose a few kilos simply to fit into wedding clothes.Eli Lilly told Reuters that Mounjaro had been approved for specific medical indications and should be used only under the supervision of a qualified healthcare professional.Novo Nordisk, meanwhile, said it discouraged self-medication with semaglutide or any deviation from its approved use.Another item in wedding checklist?The wedding industry may have added another item to the preparation checklist, but the body cannot be expected to work to the same deadline as a wedding planner. articles.title: Teenager's leg amputated after Barry Island stabbing on bank holiday, court hears
articles.summary: Idris Ahmed attacked the 17-year-old after he acted "as a peacemaker" between two groups.
articles.body:
A 17-year-old boy had to have his leg amputated following an "unprovoked" stabbing during a bank holiday trip to Barry Island.

Newport Crown Court heard that the boy, who cannot be named because of his age, was with a group of friends in May 2026 when the incident happened.

Idris Ahmed attacked the teenager after he acted "as a peacemaker" between two groups before the altercation.

The 19-year-old from Riverside, Cardiff denies one charge of grievous bodily harm with intent, one charge of inflicting grievous bodily harm and a charge of possessing a knife.

The jury heard the 17-year-old victim was with friends who were all "having fun, drinking and throwing water and sand at each other" on 25 May, which was a "bright sunny day".

Nuhu Gobir, prosecuting, said Ahmed also went to Barry Island that day with friends and the two groups eventually started to interact close to a rocky area of the beach, with one of the 17-year-old's friends becoming uneasy about the other group.

"The complainant spoke with them and tried to be diplomatic - he was a peacemaker", Gobir said.

The different groups eventually shook hands but the court heard Ahmed returned moments later and stabbed the teenager in the leg "without warning".

"The defendant approached the complainant from behind, pulled a knife from his shorts and stabbed him to his leg without any warning," Gobir said.

He added the 17-year-old victim did not see the person who stabbed him but witnesses did, including those who knew Ahmed.

In the moment after the attack, the 17-year-old fell to the ground and looked pale, saying: "I am going, I feel myself going."

Ahmed then fled the scene and discarded the knife close to a nearby building, an act seen by an eyewitness who later identified the 19-year-old in an identity parade.

Before he threw the object Ahmed was heard saying: "I need to dash this."

He was also captured fleeing the scene by a woman who was taking selfies on the beach with her partner.

The court heard the 17-year-old was taken by air ambulance to the University Hospital of Wales in Cardiff, and had sustained an injury to the main blood vessel in his right leg, with one artery completely blocked.

Despite several transfusions, oxygen was not flowing properly to the leg and a decision was reached that an amputation was necessary.

The court heard the teenager had a through knee amputation - removing the lower half of the leg.

Ahmed was questioned by police shortly after the incident and responded "no comment" to most of the questions, but the court heard he denied stabbing anyone and said he knew nothing about the incident and was released.

Gobir said it was the prosecution's case that the defendant was the person responsible for stabbing the victim and "that he must have intended to cause him really serious harm by stabbing him to a vital part of his body with such a dangerous weapon".

The court was then shown CCTV from various cameras around Barry Island Pleasure Park area showing the groups of teenagers on the day of the incident.

On Tuesday afternoon, the jury were played a police interview with the victim where he explained more about the incident.

He said that some of his female friends had started talking to a large group of boys as they sat on the rocks.

He said that a male friend had started to get nervous, believing he "might have had a problem with these boys" but the teenager tried to calm the situation with the other group.

He said he did not know the reason why he was attacked, describing the sensation of being stabbed as "like a punch", adding "I knew straight away I had been stabbed".

He said it was a "sharp pain" but it "didn't really sting how you'd expect it to".

He described how he was in and out of consciousness as he was taken to the hospital but remembered seeing his friend being attacked by another man with a plastic shovel. He said in total he had to have four surgeries on his leg.

articles.title: Dietitian Reveals the Healthiest Type of Canned Tuna
articles.summary: Canned tuna is a quick source of protein, but which type is best for you? A dietitian reveals what to look for in healthier canned tuna and which types to limit.
articles.body: If you’re looking to eat more fish, canned tuna is a no-brainer. Love it or hate it, this shelf-stable fish is one of the healthiest foods you can keep in your pantry. It’s a quick, easy source of protein and other beneficial nutrients. Plus, it’s affordable. Compared to other types of tinned fish, canned tuna is by far the most popular, especially in the United States. At the grocery store, you’ll find shelves stacked with cans of different tuna varieties. The actual species of fish can vary, as well as how it’s packed and the added ingredients. You’ll see labels like “albacore” and “skipjack.” Some tuna is canned solid, whereas other types get broken up into chunks. Perhaps you don’t pay much mind to these differences, since it’s all the same fish in different packaging anyway. However, there’s a catch. Not all canned tuna is equal, nutritionally. Which is the healthiest type? Does it matter whether the tuna is packed in water or oil? And what’s the difference between “white” and “light” tuna, anyway? We spoke to a dietitian to answer your canned tuna questions. Is Canned Tuna Good for You? Tuna is one of the most widely consumed types of seafood in the world. It’s technically an umbrella term that refers to dozens of species of large saltwater fish. The most common types of tuna commercially fished and canned include skipjack (also known as “light” tuna), albacore or “white” tuna, and yellowfin tuna, TODAY.com reported previously. Just like fresh tuna, the canned version is packed with nutrients. “It’s a great source of protein, with about 22 grams in just three ounces,” registered dietitian and author Frances Largeman-Roth tells TODAY.com. The lean, high-quality protein in tuna can help support muscle growth and repair, keep you feeling full and support weight management. The latest Dietary Guidelines for Americans (2025-2030) recommend prioritizing protein at every meal and aiming to get 1.2–1.6 grams of protein per kilogram of body weight per day. Canned tuna is an efficient way to get a significant amount of protein and meet your intake goals, Largeman-Roth notes. Most tuna is relatively low in fat and calories, and naturally carbohydrate-free. Skipjack tuna tends to be the leanest variety, whereas albacore tuna contains a slightly higher fat content. Whichever you opt for, the fats you get from tuna are very healthy. “Canned tuna provides a significant amount of heart-protective omega-3 fatty acids,” says Largeman-Roth. These include DHA and EPA, essential fatty acids that the body can’t make enough of on its own, so we need to get them from foods, such as fish. The omega-3s in tuna can also support brain, eye and skin health. In addition to protein and omega-3s, canned tuna is a good source of vitamin B12, which supports energy metabolism and nervous system function, vitamin D and selenium. Canned tuna is also one of the most accessible forms of fish. “According to the American Heart Association, we’re supposed to be eating two or more servings of fish each week,” says Largeman-Roth — but nearly 90% of Americans fall short of this. Between the high retail price of fresh fish and lack of skill or confidence cooking with seafood, “many of us are not eating enough,” says Largeman-Roth. “Canned tuna is a great way to meet the intake recommendations and get the nutrients you need in an affordable way,” she adds. The Healthiest Type of Canned Tuna All canned tuna can offer important nutrients with health benefits. However, the species of tuna makes a difference. The healthiest type of canned tuna tends to be skipjack, says Largeman-Roth, because it’s a smaller species of fish which is naturally lower in mercury — that’s why the U.S. Food and Drug Administration considers skipjack a “best choice” for regular consumption (two to three times a week). Other species of canned tuna, like albacore or yellowfin, can still be part of a healthy diet, but should be consumed less frequently. What’s added to the tuna and the liquid it’s packed in also matter nutritionally, says Largeman-Roth. Better-for-you canned tuna options share a few qualities: Packed in water or extra virgin olive oilNo salt addedWild or safe-caught The healthiest varieties tend to contain tuna as the first and only ingredient. “I’m a big fan of tuna packed in EVOO because it really doesn’t need anything else added to it to taste great, but you can also choose water-packed tuna,” says Largeman-Roth. The olive oil provides additional heart-healthy monounsaturated fats and beneficial plant compounds, but has more calories. Canned tuna can be high in sodium, which most Americans can stand to cut back on. If you eat the entire can and mix the tuna with condiments and seasonings, this can quickly add up. “I like to go with the unsalted variety and add my own sea salt if I want,” says Largeman-Roth. When possible, try to opt for wild-caught fish over farmed varieties, which often have slightly more nutrients, TODAY.com previously reported. “I do recommend choosing tuna brands that do rigorous mercury testing on their fish, especially for kids and women who are pregnant or breastfeeding,” says Largeman-Roth. Canned Tuna to Limit or Avoid Most types of canned tuna can be part of a healthy diet when eaten in moderation. However, Largeman-Roth recommends limiting varieties that come with unnecessary calories, sodium and additives. Tuna that’s packed in vegetable oil — which is a blend of refined oils like soy, corn or canola — will be higher in fats that offer fewer benefits than tuna in heart-healthy olive oil. Additionally, try to limit or avoid canned tuna with a lot of added salt and flavorings. “Some varieties have more than 400 mg of sodium per serving,” Largeman-Roth notes. Generally, the fewer ingredients, the better. If the nutrition label on a can of tuna contains a long list of words you can’t pronounce, consider a different variety. Which Canned Tuna is Highest in Mercury? Nearly all fish contains trace amounts of methylmercury, a toxin found in water which accumulates in fish’s tissues over time as they feed, per the FDA. The larger the fish, the higher on the food chain and the more mercury that builds up. When it comes to canned tuna, albacore, aka “white” tuna, is the largest species, which means it has the highest mercury content, says Largeman-Roth. Yellowfin tuna is also higher in mercury than skipjack. These are still “good choices,” per the FDA, but you should limit your consumption of albacore and yellowfin tuna to two times per week (or once per week if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding). (Technically, bigeye and bluefin tuna contain the most mercury of any species and should be avoided, but these are very rarely available canned). For most people, the exposure to mercury from eating fish is not a concern, per the FDA. However, high levels of mercury may be harmful to pregnant women and young children, because it can affect the developing nervous system. That’s why the FDA recommends pregnant women and young children choose lower mercury fish to eat regularly. Always talk to your doctor if you have concerns or questions about eating canned tuna. Healthiest Ways to Eat Canned Tuna Canned tuna is delicious and versatile, says Largeman-Roth. You can enjoy the tuna on its own with a few simple ingredients, like lemon juice and fresh herbs. It can also be added to recipes to boost the protein content and make for a more filling, substantial meal. Try these canned tuna recipes to get started: High-protein tuna salad with Greek yogurtTuna macaroni pasta saladNiçoise-style tuna grain bowlsTuna kimbapMediterranean tuna sandwiches
